title: A calming corrective to AI concerns
text:
A calming corrective to AI concerns
Loading...
Warnings about the potential dangers of unfettered artificial intelligence development have reached their highest decibel levels yet. There is deep – and vociferous – concern among tech experts and the public about “rogue” AI and fears it could lead to humanity’s possible extinction.
Last Tuesday, an AI researcher’s online resignation announcement – which garnered 120 million views within 24 hours – claimed AI firms are “gambling with our lives.” A colleague at Anthropic shared his own fears and prediction about AI’s threat to human existence in the next decade. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a call for all AI firms to slow down the pace of development, embed independent safety auditors, and cooperate globally to design standards and guardrails.
The heads of OpenAI, SpaceX, and Google DeepMind agreed with Dr. Amodei. Some critics and competitors, however, view this unity as a ploy among the “frontier labs” to control market share and influence current and anticipated stock valuations.
Whether underlying motivations are sincere or not, ongoing public discussion about AI development and regulation is important and timely. But allowing a sense of urgency to tip into panic is not helpful – nor is it necessary.
In fact, a growing chorus of voices among industry insiders as well as social scientists is calling for a different kind of deceleration: It’s time to put the brakes on apocalyptic assumptions and patterns of thinking around AI’s inevitable superiority, they say. Rather than “doomerism,” they urge approaching the many unknowns of this rapidly evolving technology with a combination of curiosity, some skepticism, and confidence in humanity’s creativity and problem-solving capacities.
“The widespread belief that AI will define our future has not only a predictive but also a potentially self-fulfilling quality,” according to an article in the academic journal Anthropological Theory. “AI’s apparent autonomy functions less as a property of the technology itself than as a collectively sustained form of belief,” is its somewhat startling observation. Drifting along with this current of thought, the article indicates, tends to “naturalize AI’s purported inevitability,” while obscuring elements such as systemic incentives or individual biases that inform AI design, production, and management.
Many AI executives and researchers, The New York Times reported last week, “believe that existential risk is a serious problem in part because they have always believed it.” And, according to the Pew Research Center, nearly two-thirds of Americans worry that AI is advancing too fast – and have little confidence in the United States government’s ability to regulate AI or in firms’ approach to responsible model development.
The way we frame public conversations and thinking can stem the spread of such concerns – and calmly correct them, in the view of Melanie Mitchell, author of “Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans.” She has cautioned against using “evocative terms” that characterize AI as possessing humanlike traits and emotions.
Referring to recent hacking incidents involving AI agents, Dr. Mitchell wrote in a recent newsletter on Substack, “It’s useful to consider a more prosaic description of what actually happened.” Those events were not about “loss of control … or any kind of human-like agency on the part of AI models,” she observed. Rather, they were failures in engineering, testing conditions, and training models.
Potential solutions will likely need nuanced regulation and international cooperation – such as at the upcoming China-U.S. summit. But more challenging and important, according to Dr. Mitchell, is adjusting expectations of AI, to see it “not as a moral agent, but as a set of tools to enhance human thriving.”
A necessary prelude to that, she asserted, is “embracing our own human agency.”
